newsitem.title: UK: Jewelers sell more gold, investors buy less.
newsitem.headline: Jewelers sell more gold, investors buy less.

text.p: Gold jewellery demand was at a record high last year but demand by investors waned, the World Gold Council said Wednesday.
The producer-sponsored group, which monitors countries that account for 75 percent of gold demand, said 2,242 metric tons of gold jewellery were purchased in 1996 compared with 2,231 tons in 1995.
But investors bought only 322 tons last year, a drop of 25 percent from 432 tons the previous year.
Overall consumption fell 102 tons to 2,642 tons, off 4 percent from a year earlier, it said.
George Milling-Stanley, Gold Council manager for gold market analysis, said that the drop in investor demand was not a sign of gold losing its role as an investment asset.
"This is not indicative of a longer term trend. Demand last year was a logical response to bizarre movements in exchange rates," he said.
Japan, Germany and Austria all benefitted from favourable exchange rates, which meant the price of gold was at an 18-year low in Japan and a 12-year low in German marks.
"In 1996 investment demand has fallen back to more normal levels commensurate with early 1990s and late 1980s," Milling-Stanley said.
Much of Latin America and former Soviet bloc countries are not monitored by the World Gold Council.

"Gold demand in 1996 remained very close to the previous year's record high level, in spite of a drop in investment demand. The overall 1996 performance is a testament to the strength of jewellery demand," the gold council said.
Jewellery consumption totalled 2,242 tons just above the record set the year before and remained robust so far in 1997, it said.
Gold demand increased in the Middle East and the developing markets of Asia and Latin America as well as in the United States and Europe.
Demand in Japan fell 41 percent against 1995 -- largely reflecting the decline in investor interest.
Gold devotees in India, the world's largest importer of the precious metal, bought more than 500 tons for the first time, which was up 6 percent from a year earlier.
Milling-Stanley noted that high Indian demand was continuing into 1997.
A key factor was the recent liberalisation programme by the Indian government that allowed non resident Indians to bring home up to 22 pounds of gold every six months.
However gold demand in China, once the great hope for ever increasing consumption declined by 7 percent to 371.4 tons.
Part of the reason was the increasing demand put on the more affluent population's disposable income as the Chinese government provided fewer services than in its harder line Communist days.
"After the death of Deng (Chinese leader Deng Xiaoping last week) it is possible to see continuing liberalisation of the socio-political environment," said Milling-Stanley.
"But you may also see more liberalisation of the gold market which could help to offset that decline (in consumer spending)," he said.
